To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the distribution of plants in oceanic islands is shaped by dispersal syndroms, 2) plants with dispersal syndrom related to long distance dispersal (LDS) have a greater distribution than plants without dispersal syndrom and 3) the importance of dispersal syndrom in the Canary Islands is greater than in other archipelagos.

species with LDD syndrome traits (endozoochorous and epizoochory, and thalassocory in the Canary Islands) have significantly wider distribution across the archipelago than those with unspecilized diaspores, and that the importance of LDD in shaping the distribution of the native flora in the Canary Islands is stronger than in other archipelagos.

understanding the role of plant dispersal syndromesin shaping the biogeography of island plant communities.
understanding the role of long-distance dispersals in shaping the distribution and diversity of plant communities in the Canary Islands.

understanding how the capacity of plants (species) to reach new islands, and to colonize them, is determined by their specific diaspore traits, historically called dispersa The capacity of plants to disperse their diaspores (fruits, seeds and other propagules) is a fundamental factor in determining their ability to colonize new islands.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LDD syndroms matter for inter-island plant distributions, but the importance of LDD in shaping plant distributions across archipelagos may vary depending on the particular biogeographic context.

the role of LID dispersal syndroms in shaping interisland plant distribution is highly dependent on the archipelagos considered, and the specific biogeographical and evolutionary histories of each one.
dispersal-related traits of diaspores have a strong influence on the biogeographic patterns of the native flora of lowland xeric vegetation in the Canary Islands.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dispersal syndrome of the plant diaspores is a key factor for shaping their distribution across oceanic islands, but the relative importance of each syndrome varies across archipelagos, probably as a function of the specific dispersal filters operating in each one of them.

the dispersal syndroms of plants matter in shaping their distribution in oceanic islands.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of LLD syndromes in plant distribution between oceanic islands is far from trivial and that their importance varies across archipelagos.
diaspore traits related to LDD are important in determining plant distribution across the Canarian archipelago.
the capacity of a plant to reach a new island is not determined by the number of seeds it produces but by the traits of its diaspores.
